headline: Marvell to acquire Lumentum in $115 billion all-stock deal, boosting AI optical tech
summary: The $115 billion all-stock deal combines two major data center optics players, positioning Marvell as a leader in AI optical interconnects. It is reportedly the second-largest tech transaction deal ever.
details: Marvell Technology Inc. has signed a definitive merger agreement to acquire Lumentum for an enterprise value of $115 billion. This combines two of the biggest players in the data center optics market into one company.

Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each share they own, valued at about $1,132 per share. This represents a 23.9% premium over Lumentum's unaffected closing price on October 28.

Marvell's current shareholders will hold about 67% of the combined company, with Lumentum's shareholders holding about 33%. This agreement is reportedly the second-largest tech transaction deal ever, after the SpaceX-xAI merger.
Both company boards have unanimously approved the deal, which is expected to close in the first half of 2028, pending regulatory and shareholder approval.

This acquisition significantly expands Marvell's optical infrastructure portfolio. It follows its $10 billion acquisition of Inphi in 2021 and the $3.5 billion purchase of Celestial AI in February 2026.

All three mergers and acquisitions involved companies handling different parts of critical AI infrastructure: optical connectivity. As AI infrastructure scales, optical connectivity is increasingly important for moving vast amounts of data.

Marvell, already a supplier of optical DSPs, silicon photonics, and high-speed SerDes, is positioning itself as a major provider of optical interconnect technologies. This spans scale-across and scale-out networking to emerging scale-up and scale-in connections.

Modern AI data centers house thousands of interconnected accelerators exchanging enormous volumes of data. Copper interconnects hit physical limits at around one to two meters, making optics the industry's solution for data movement.

Optical transceivers and fiber optics initially replaced copper for inter-rack connections and beyond. These components convert electrical signals into light for transmission and back again at the receiving end.

The industry is also advancing to bring optics directly into accelerator packages with co-packaged and near-packaged optics. This approach places the photonic integrated circuit (PIC) chip directly on the switch or accelerator package, shrinking the electrical path.

headline: Agility Robotics goes public via SPAC, raising $465M for humanoid robot development
summary: Agility Robotics, known for its bipedal Digit robots, is going public through a reverse-merger, raising $465 million to accelerate the development and deployment of its next-generation Digit 5 robots.
details: Agility Robotics is set to go public via a reverse-merger, securing $465 million in new capital from retail investors and private funding. This transaction will be facilitated through a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC), making it the first pure humanoid robot company on the stock market.

Spun out of Oregon State University in 2015, Agility focused on developing robots capable of safe bipedal locomotion. Unlike competitors, the company prioritizes practical, repetitive industrial tasks over flashy demonstrations.

Currently, Agility deploys its Digit robots in industrial settings for nine customers, including GXO and Toyota, primarily moving heavy totes. Despite doing 'real work,' the company reported only $174,000 in revenue and $362 million in losses during the first half of 2026.

The company has secured $300 million in planned contracts from 30 customers for its upcoming Digit 5 robot. This new model is designed to operate safely around humans, expanding its utility beyond isolated work cells.

Digit 5 prototypes are expected to be unveiled at CES 2027, with wide availability slated for the end of that year. The robot must meet undisclosed targets for throughput, uptime, and placement accuracy to fulfill these contracts.

Agility's business model includes a robot-as-a-service option, projecting annual savings of $100,000 per robot for companies. The ultimate success hinges on Digit 5's capabilities and operational efficiency, including uptime and task accuracy.

Key challenges include rapidly acquiring new customers for Digit 5 and enhancing the robot's complex manipulation skills. Prospective clients must invest $500,000 for an on-site proof of concept before full-scale deployment.

Agility leverages 65,000 hours of real operational data from customer facilities to accelerate Digit's training. This extensive real-world data provides a significant advantage in developing reliable general autonomy compared to simulation-based approaches.
